rv.q: So it's a relief and a special pleasure to report that Mayer, in a square-cornered turn from his smart-rock productions of "Spring Awakening" and "American Idiot," has joined playwright Peter Parnell to change an unworkable plot into a more-than-serviceable gender-bending framework.

Harry Connick Jr. and his castmates make magic with the melodious score, but despite an adventurous gender-switch, the problematic 1965 musical remains as over-complicated as ever in this radical rethink.

The diagnosis is in for Harry Connick Jr.'s Broadway musical about a psychiatrist undergoing a psychic meltdown: It needs more time on the couch. A completely reworked 'On a Clear Day You Can See Forever,' which opened Sunday at the St.
This revival of the 1965. Lerner and Loewe musical is a gorgeous mess—emphasis on gorgeous.
Connick may have had a Tony-nominated turn in 2006's "The Pajama Game," but here he can barely carry his songs, let alone the show.

The craggy crooner, who plays opposite the gorgeously voiced Chicago star Jessie Mueller in a troubled and perplexing show that is hardly the best vehicle for her Broadway debut, has a physical resemblance to the handsome former vice president, and he also embodies some of Gore's signature stiffness.

Though done up to resemble a psychedelic fun house (the sanitized, perky kind that brings to mind middle-of-the-road rock album covers from the late 1960s and early ’70s), this “Clear Day” still has the approximate fun quotient of a day in an M.R.I. machine.
The new On a Clear Day might be an overambitious mess were it not for the winning performances and luscious music.
Surely, that’s not what’s wanted for a show that sets out to entertain — and so often does exactly that.
Well, you get the picture, even if audiences may find it spotty.
The result is the depressing misfire currently at the St. James Theatre, starring a distinctly ill-at-ease Harry Connick Jr.
Hideous to look at and hard on the ears despite star Harry Connick Jr., the Broadway revival of “On a Clear Day You Can See Forever” is dead on arrival.
But none of these satisfactions are enough to make 'On A Clear Day' much more than an intermittently entertaining oddity.
